opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What makes this compelling to me is really a question of efficiency and access. Training a foundation model from scratch on satellite imagery is enormously expensive. You need huge amounts of data, a lot of compute, and frankly a lot of energy, and only a handful of organizations in the world can afford to do that. At the same time, we already have very strong foundation models trained on natural images, and they've learned a lot of general visual knowledge: edges, textures, shapes, compositional structure. So the question we asked was, why throw all of that away and start from zero?

Remote sensing data is different, of course. You have multispectral and hyperspectral bands well beyond RGB, you have SAR, you have a top-down perspective, different resolutions, temporal series. But a lot of the underlying visual representation is still transferable. If we can distill or transfer the knowledge from these large general-purpose models into a remote sensing model, and then adapt it to the specific modalities of Earth observation, we can get a model that performs competitively at a fraction of the cost and carbon footprint.

For me that's also an important point about democratization. Earth observation matters for climate monitoring, agriculture, disaster response, and biodiversity, and the people working on these problems are often in research institutions or public agencies that don't have hyperscaler budgets. If we can show that knowledge transfer lets you build strong remote sensing foundation models more cheaply, that opens the door for many more groups to build and adapt these models for their own needs. So it's a mix of scientific curiosity, how much knowledge really transfers across domains, and a very practical motivation to make this technology more sustainable and more accessible.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. What makes it compelling, honestly, is a mismatch that's been bugging me for years. In computer vision, foundation models trained on huge amounts of internet imagery have become the default starting point for almost everything. You take a pretrained backbone, you fine-tune, and you get strong results with relatively little labeled data. In remote sensing, we have the opposite situation: an enormous amount of unlabeled data coming down from satellites every day, petabytes of it, but comparatively little labeled data, and the labels we do have are expensive, domain specific, and often tied to a particular sensor or a particular region.

So the natural question is, can we get the benefits of foundation models without having to train one from scratch on satellite data? Training from scratch is costly, both in compute and in the engineering effort to curate the data, and the remote sensing community doesn't have the same resources as the big labs. And satellite imagery is also genuinely different from natural images. You have different spectral bands, not just RGB, you have radar from Sentinel-1, you have very different spatial statistics, there's no canonical "up" in an image, objects are tiny. So you can't just naively take an ImageNet model and expect it to work.

What's interesting about knowledge transfer is that it sits in the middle. We take what a large pretrained vision model has already learned about structure, textures, edges, compositional patterns, and we ask how much of that is reusable for the Earth observation domain, and how do we adapt the rest. That involves things like learning how to map multispectral inputs into something the pretrained model understands, or distilling the representations into a smaller model that is tailored to satellite data. The appealing part is that you leverage the investment that's already been made at scale, and you only spend your compute on the delta, on what's specific to the domain.

And for me there's a bigger motivation behind it. Remote sensing isn't just an academic benchmark exercise. These models feed into applications like monitoring deforestation, tracking floods, estimating crop yields, assessing damage after disasters. If we can lower the barrier so that a research group or an NGO can build a capable model without a massive training budget, that has real impact. So the compelling thing is partly scientific, understanding what transfers across such different visual domains, and partly practical, making these capabilities accessible to people who actually need them.

astra-6.text:
What makes it compelling to me is that remote sensing gives us an opportunity to understand how the world is changing, but the data is quite different from the natural images we typically use to train vision models. You have different sensors, different spectral bands, and repeated observations of the same location over time. And while there’s a lot of data, getting good labels can be difficult.

So the interesting question is: how much of what a model has already learned can we transfer into that setting? Can we use those representations as a starting point, while still learning the information that’s unique to remote sensing? You want to benefit from existing models without losing what makes these observations valuable.

If we can do that well, we have a foundation that can support many different tasks, rather than building a separate model from scratch for each one. That connection between a challenging learning problem and the potential to monitor changes on Earth is what makes it exciting to me.

sol-6.1.text:
What makes it compelling to me is that we have an enormous amount of satellite data, but relatively little labeled data. And the labels are often very specific to a particular region, sensor, or point in time. So the question is: How can we transfer what a model has already learned to make that data useful without starting from scratch for every application?

Remote sensing also gives us different views of the same place—optical imagery, radar, observations across time. Knowledge transfer offers a way to connect those views and learn representations that can support many downstream tasks. You could then adapt a foundation model to monitor forests, understand agricultural changes, or assess damage with much less task-specific annotation.

For me, the exciting part is connecting that technical opportunity to observing changes on our planet at scale.
